prompt: Put the four moments of a crash reporter in order.
items: it starts before the app's own code
it keeps breadcrumbs while the app runs
on a crash, it writes the report to disk
on the next launch, it sends and deletes the report

prompt: Why does a crash reporter not send the report at the moment of the crash?

choices.text: The stores forbid network requests during a crash
choices.why: No store rule is involved.

choices.text: To batch reports and save battery
choices.why: Batching is a side effect, not the reason.

choices.text: A crashing process cannot be trusted to finish one
choices.why: Right. Writing one file is the most it can do.

choices.text: The person has to agree first
choices.why: Consent is decided before, not at the crash.

prompt: Which crash is the least likely to ever reach a reporter that sends on the next launch?

choices.why: Right. If every launch crashes, no launch sends.

choices.text: A crash during a sync in the background
choices.why: Saved, and sent when the app next opens.

choices.text: A crash in the settings screen
choices.why: The next launch sends it.

choices.text: A crash on an old phone
choices.why: The age of the phone does not stop the next launch.

prompt: In the lesson's capture, what did the person see when the planner crashed?

choices.text: An error dialog with the stack
choices.why: Nothing was printed at all.
That came on the next launch.

choices.text: A message that a report was sent
choices.why: It was sent on the next launch, silently.
Right. Exit status 1 and no output.

prompt: Which field of the lesson's report is most likely to carry personal data by accident?

choices.why: It names nobody by design.
Right. They hold whatever the app wrote into them.
It is the same for everybody on that build.
A type name such as TypeError is not personal.

prompt: What does `sendPending` do with a report when the network is down?

choices.text: Deletes it, since it cannot be sent
choices.why: It deletes only after the server accepts.

choices.text: Leaves it for the next launch
choices.why: Right. The catch is there for exactly that.
Nothing is shown.

choices.text: Retries it every second until it works
choices.why: That would block the app's start.

prompt: Which of these fields in the lesson's report count people without naming them? Choose every one.

choices.why: Right. Random, and kept per installation.
They describe actions, not who did them.
A time counts nothing.
The system version describes the device, not a person.

prompt: Match each platform to the symbol file its release build produces.

pairs.right: a source map, from Metro or Hermes

prompt: A team rebuilds the commit of 1.5.0 to upload symbols it forgot. Why will the crashes still be unreadable?

choices.why: They do not expire.
Even with the same code, the mapping differs.

choices.text: The crash reporter refuses late uploads
choices.why: Late is fine; a different build is not.
Right. Symbols belong to the exact build that shipped.

prompt: In Sentry, the hook that lets the app strip personal data from a report before it leaves the phone is called ___.
What turns crash reports from Data Not Linked to You into Data Linked to You?

choices.why: Right. Lesson 5's line.
The product does not decide it; the data does.
Symbols describe the code, not the person.
A model names no person.

prompt: What is Android vitals' overall threshold for the user-perceived crash rate, in per cent?
One person hits the same crash forty times this week; nobody else crashes. Which rate moves more?

choices.why: One person out of many barely moves it.
They disagree exactly here.
Right. Forty crashed sessions, one person.
Grouping merges reports into an issue; the rates still count.

prompt: How does a crash reporter decide that two reports are the same issue?

choices.text: By the error type and the top frames of the stack
choices.why: Right. With varying parts such as addresses removed.
Time says nothing about the cause.
That counts people; it does not group causes.
One version has many different crashes.

prompt: The planner is at 0.6% crashes overall and 9% on one popular phone model. What does Android vitals make of it?

choices.text: Nothing; the overall rate is under 1.09%
choices.why: The per-model threshold is separate.

choices.text: The app is removed from the store
choices.why: Visibility is affected; removal is not the rule.

choices.text: Above the 8% threshold on that model
choices.why: Right. Play may warn people with that phone.
9% is over the per-model 8%.

prompt: Issues in the crash reporter should be sorted by what, according to the lesson?

choices.why: One person can send hundreds.
Right. Newest release first.
Old issues are not the first to fix.
That says nothing about harm.

prompt: A Swift team ships 1.5.0 and its crash reports show only addresses. What did it skip?

choices.why: Breadcrumbs do not name functions.
R8 is Android's.
That identifies people, not functions.

choices.text: Uploading the dSYM of the build that shipped
choices.why: Right. Addresses map to names only through it.
